utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you attend that presentation?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: No, I did not. I was not present at the presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Do you know who was in attendance at the presentation?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I do recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court where you got the document from.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I would have received the document from OPs centre at Sector South headquarters, either from Major Balfour or Major Dussault, the operation officers?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you retrieve that document on the 22nd of August?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I don't recall, sir. That is the date that is on my memo or my short note to Colonel Leslie. With that in mind, that it is probably the same date that I retrieved the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that basis, I would move for the admission, understanding that the probative value, of course, can be slightly effected since we don't who drafted it. Nevertheless, this was a communication of information relevant to this case, submitted from the HQ Sector South to UNCRO in Zagreb. On that basis, I would move for its admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just find it astonishing that we're asking to move a document that doesn't exist and that nobody has into evidence based on a cover letter. It is mind-boggling to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not sure what the meaning is that the document doesn't exist. Clearly, the witness has already testified he got it from at least someone. He believes it is the OPs centre in the HQ Sector South. He transmitted it to a higher authority in Zagreb. Clearly, it is a roughly contemporaneous record of what someone in the HQ Sector South had presented to someone else. The Court can take it for what it is worth; nevertheless, I think it is information that would assist the Court in making its own determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, and with all due respect to Captain Berikoff, we can't cross-examine the man on a document that he has no knowledge as to who prepared, how it was prepared, and on what basis the document was prepared. Merely going in there and pulling something out and sending to Leslie doesn't qualify or authenticate this document. If, in fact, this was done by Leslie, why did the Prosecution not put it to Colonel Leslie when he was here? Heavens knows he was here for long enough. Now, there are comments in here frankly that are extremely prejudicial. And, again, with all due respect to Captain Berikoff, I am sure when I asked about those, he will simply say, "I don't know. I don't know where this document came from, I don't have a source for it, and I don't know where those comments come from." It is simply not sufficient to say that somebody, at some someplace, at sometime drafted a document. Mr. Berikoff happened to grab it and then sends it up to UNCRO headquarters in Zagreb and that thereby authenticates it. If this is an witness that did it, the OTP should go found out who did it, so he or she can come back in and defend the contents of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly agree with Mr. Kehoe. He is not able to cross-examine this particular witness on the content of the document; nevertheless, that goes to the weight to be accorded to the Court. It is clearly a statement which, as I indicated, is roughly contemporaneous with the events which it purports to relate to. It is something some one in the UN HQ compound said about what happened. On that basis, they could use it to cross-examine other witnesses to see if the agree with it or do not agree with it. We have no information that it was drafted by Colonel Leslie. And if we had, we certainly would have submitted it through him. We simply don't know who drafted, but we do know that it was sent by Mr. Berikoff to Colonel Leslie upon Colonel Leslie' request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have information that it was not drafted by Colonel Leslie?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We don't have information one way or the other. However, I can tell the Court that this was -- I believe came to us attached to General Leslie's statements; although, I don't believe he indicated to us that he was able to authenticate the content of it, which is why it was not offered through him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if he is not able to authenticate, then you have information that he was the author, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe that's a circumstance which I could safely assume, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, then, the answer to my last question could have been shorter; it could have been "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just, frankly, it is a document. Who knows when it was created? I mean, it doesn't have a particular date on it. And with all due respect to my learned friend across the well, I mean, the OTP has at least some preliminary burden to tell not only the Chamber but to the Defence who is responsible for this, so that we can have a meaningful dialogue. Again, with all due respect, Captain, he doesn't know, so it is not going to a meaningful dialogue, and the OTP just throws this document across the transom. Then they say, well, like it or not, here it is. I think that that is not a pursuit of facts that are detailed here, and I will tell you, Your Honour, that there are some very prejudicial comments in this document that need to be addressed. And it is simply not asking the OTP after 13 years of investigation to find out who authored this document. There has to be a limited circle of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber -- Mr. Russo, I heard you saying something when I had my earphones off. I don't know what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I had just one brief response, but if the Court has already made up its mind, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have not made up our mind as a matter of fact. But if it is a brief comment, then I make take it that the Defence has a brief comment as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I agree with Mr. Kehoe that there is limited circle of people who could have authored this document, which is why I believe there is some probative value to be attached to it; however, we simply don't know who among that circle of people it was who drafted it. Nevertheless, the circumstances in which it came to the OTP, which I now can address, for example, to someone showing up at a crime scene, finding a journal on the floor of a crime scene, they can authenticate what is in the journalism. Nevertheless, the fact that it was found at the crime scene nevertheless makes it evidence that the Court should see. This document is no different. We don't know who authored it, how accurate it is; nevertheless, we do know that it came out of the one location from which the UN was reporting the most contemporaneous information regarding events in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now see all three. I think, I saw Ms. Higgins first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... sorry. I just didn't see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there was a whole queue behind you. Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly, on behalf of Mr. Cermak, we joint the objection to this document on several bases. Primarily, the first being the rule has been incorrectly stated by Mr. Russo. If this Chamber is to descend to the levels of allowing documentation to come in mainly and purely on the basis that it would assist this Court, then we would start to apply rules which are not within the rule books themselves. And it would reduce the levels of admissibility to levels of incomprehensibility. This witness cannot speak on any level or to any degree through no fault of his own to this document. And I fail to see the basis despite the valiant attempts arguably by Mr. Russo upon which this document could come before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have nothing to add to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last comment, Judge. I find this most recent analysis by Mr. Russo simply astonishing that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean that he considers UN circles to be the crime scene; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I find it happening upon a report. Let us extrapolate this out and look at it in the general criminal sector with police departments. It happens to be some report that is unsigned, undated, and it happens to have evidence that is involved in a --or could be conceivably involved in some criminal matter. And without any description of the author or naming of the author as to where this information comes from, the Prosecution has submitted that this -- that this document should be admitted into evidence with none of the attendant information to check on authenticity. If that is the standard of documents under which documents should come in, I have to join in the comments made by Ms. Higgins that there is no standard, and that is basically what Mr. Russo has put before this Court. There is it simply no standard. They found it, it's around, somebody wrote it, we don't know who, we don't know when, but it comes in. Oh, by the way, Defence, you can't cross-examine anybody on the content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, Mr. Kuzmanovic, Ms. Higgins, and Mr. Kehoe, the Chamber will consider the admission into evidence of the document. And, therefore, it will be marked for identification for the time being. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P760, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't if the Court is of a mind for a recess at that point. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, the debate was so interesting that I forgot to look at the clock, with my apologies for all those suffering from it. We will have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, I'd now like to ask you some questions regarding some specific events that you witnessed during and after Operation Storm. Can you tell Court whether you took a trip to Knin hospital on 4 August?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what the circumstances of that trip were.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: The first trip I took to the Knin hospital was with the SMEDLO, the Senior Medical Officer. We went down to see if, in fact, we could offer assistance to any of the wounded people in the hospital or with the medical staff. When we got to the hospital, we were turned around and our help was refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You indicated that -- well, let me ask first: On that trip to the hospital, did you see any ARSK tanks positioned at or near the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I am not aware of any military position near the hospital at that time. No, I did not see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, see an ARSK tank anywhere inside the town of Knin on any of the trips you made either on 4th or 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: In Knin itself, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You indicated that on the first trip -- in your last answer, on the first trip that you took to the hospital, can you tell the Court how many times you went to the hospital on the 4th and the 5th?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I believe, on the 4th, I went to the hospital twice, or may I refer it my notes, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Sure. And while you're doing that, can you please just let the Court know what exactly it is what you're referring to when you check it.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Okay. I'm referring to the daily journal marked 17 July until 6 September, and I'm looking at the entry for the 4th of August, which is a Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And just for the Court's benefit, that's Exhibit P748.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Okay. That was the one trip when we went to the hospital, like I said, to offer assistance. I believe I made a couple of trips that day. With -- with me on the trip were a number of people, including, as I said, the Senior Medical Officer; as well, I believe the Jordanian Chief of Staff. And I'm not certain if General Leslie was with us at that time or not. He may, in fact, have been, because I know he came with us on one occasion to the hospital where he went inside and I stood in the parking lot. Following departure from the hospital, I was tasked to go to the Jordanian Chief of Staff's residence to pick up his luggage. When -- on our way to the Chief of Staff's residence, we were fired upon by an ARSK soldier who had a hand-held rocket launcher. He fired at the -- at our APC and missed. I know that General Leslie was not with us at that time, but I do know that one occasion -- I believe it was on the 4th. On the 5th, I'm not aware of him going to the hospital to go inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you go to the hospital on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: No. I did not go to the hospital on the 5th of August. In the morning, I was preoccupied with the casualties and -- and the deceased at the intersection. At 12.10 on the 5th, the Croat Puma Brigade, or members of, had come to the gate with their tanks and stopped us from any movement outside the compound. If, in fact, any carriers or any personnel went downtown on the 5th in the morning, it was without my knowledge because I was tasked to do numerous other things. So I was not aware of other vehicles. However, after 12.00 that day, nothing left the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you please refer to your third statement at page 14?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: What tab is that, please, Mr. Russo?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That is tab 3, I believe, in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And this is, again, for reference, Exhibit D284, at page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Beginning at about line 7, you're discussing a Serb doctor, and I believe that this, what you're talking about here, occurred on the 5th of August. You indicated that a Serb doctor from the day before approached the gate. He is asking for help at the hospital. And later on, on the following paragraph, beginning at line 18, it says: "En route to the hospital, there was still a number of dead on the street, probably in the vicinity of 20 to 30 people; and once we got back to the hospital, there were still a number of dead and wounded, approximately the same that were seen the day before." Then it says: "Though the bodies had not been removed from the previous day. We noticed at that time that hospital had, indeed, been hit by artillery. A number of the windows in the hospital were, in fact, broken. There were shell marks on the wall; as well, there were craters in the field surrounding the hospital." Looking at that portion of your third statement, which seems to reflect that you were at the hospital on the 5th, can you clarify whether or not having read that you have a memory of going to the hospital on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, I do not recall the 5th -- of going to the hospital on the 5th. My recollection of the 5th is that I was -- I was busy at the intersection with the casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. This is not contained in the supplemental information sheet. I would like to know when the Prosecution came into possession of this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: It's in the third statement, which is Exhibit D284, page 14, line 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the information that the witness did not go to the hospital, when that information came to the possession of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe I asked just asked him a few questions ago, and he said he didn't have a memory of going to the hospital on the 5th. I can just take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a moment. I think, Mr. Russo, what Mr. Kehoe would like it know is whether at any earlier moment you became aware that the testimony of the witness might be that he did not go to the hospital on the 5th of August. Is that, Mr. Kehoe, what you were looking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I misunderstood the question. I spoke to the witness yesterday evening after he met with members of the Defence, at which time he indicated to me he was unsure at what time or whether he went to the hospital on the 4th or the 5th, and I believe I thought it was a matter that needed calculation for the Court. I apologise if that was not communicated to the Defence; however, I think it is it pretty clear from what the witness said in court today that he doesn't have a specific recollection of whether he went to the hospital on the 5th. That's why I thought I would take him to this portion of his statement and find out if could address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, we're certainly entitled to that disclosure about that. We got three single-spaced pages of disclosures, and that very important detail has not been provided by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what time and what date that was disclosed to you. But, Mr. Russo, if you found this information, even late yesterday evening, I think we're all working day and night, so, therefore, you should have disclosed this to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. It was my understanding from the witness that it was during his conversation with the Defence that he became uncertain, and that this was communicated to him by the Defence that he was uncertain. I apologise. I didn't send it either the Cermak Defence or Markac Defence, but it was my understanding that at least the Gotovina Defence had notice of his confusion regarding that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you're awareness and you're being informed about it in a conversation with the witness is something different than the Defence finding out about these matters. It's your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, can you explain to the Court why in your third statement, on page 14, you discuss a trip to the hospital and observations that were made on a trip to the hospital on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: No, I can't explain the 5th of August. I do know that, on one occasion, General Leslie did come with us to the hospital. When we got to the hospital he went inside the hospital; I stayed in the parking lot. I do not recall, and I'm uncertain, if it is the trip with the SMEDLO or another trip. I do know, and I'm certain, that he came with us on one trip where he went into the hospital, and then he came out and he indicated how many wounded and dead he saw inside the hospital. That is why I put the information in my very first handwritten journal that I did. It was information given by General Leslie at the time. I know for a fact that when I left the hospital en route to the Jordanian Chief of Staff's residence to pick up his luggage from his residence, General Leslie was not with us at that time. I don't know if he had gone back to the hospital on his own at that time or if he had stayed on. But I do know that there was one occasion when I was personally there when Leslie went inside the hospital, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move now to your fourth statement, and that is Exhibit P741.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I take it that's tab 4, Mr. Russo?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That is correct. And turning to page 2, paragraph 2 of that statement, you describe your -- or you discuss your change of opinion regarding the indiscriminate nature of the shelling. And I would like you, please, to explain to the Court why it ask that you changed your opinion.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Following the offensive, I had a chance to reassess and take a look at the overall picture, because by this time I had numerous opportunities of driving through the town of Knin and in the -- and in the other -- outlying outskirts Knin itself. In my opinion, there were a number of areas that could have been considered military targets, be they strategic infrastructure-type targets or just military installations where there may have been troops. The opinion that I -- or the assessment that I came up upon was done immediately after as I had a chance to re-think things over. During the offensive itself, it seemed that it was indiscriminate because there were a large number of shells, there were a large number of rocket barrages, mortar fire, and everything. So it seemed like everything was coming in on Knin. But having reassessed it after, in fact, it is my opinion that there were, in fact, military targets, and it may not have been as indiscriminate as originally thought. There was a lot of collateral damage, and was the amount of shelling and rocket fire unnecessary? In my opinion, the answer is yes. And the reason I say that is because most of the ARSK had left the town, the civilians had evacuated the town, and those check-points that were located throughout the town were with minimal manning. So, I came of the opinion that, okay, was it indiscriminate? No. Was it unnecessary with the amount of fire that they put into the city of Knin? My opinion was yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would like to be clear about when exactly it was that your opinion changed. In your third statement, you indicate that you believed it was indiscriminate; however, there was a gap of almost 11 years between that statement and your following statement, which is your fourth statement, in which you indicate that your opinion has changed. At what time after your third statement did you come to a change of opinion?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: There was a number of times when I revisited in my mind the situation in Sector South and had -- and over -- and looked over my maps or the aerial photo and stuff like that and the photos that I took and looked at the various types of damage that existed, and that is when I formulated my own assessment that it was not indiscriminate, as other people had indicated?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you indicated that you realized that there were military targets in the area. Are there -- did you realize that there were any military targets in addition to those which were identified by you on the map and in your statements?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Prior to the offensive on -- on Knin, no, I was not aware of other military targets, because I had just arrived in country a few weeks prior to, and I did not have the opportunity to drive up and down the streets of Knin. My task, when I first got there, was to go outside of Knin and see what forces on either -- either side that I would encounter. So it was not my task to go up and down the streets of Knin and see what military installations were there. I knew the main military installations on the main road, the main barracks, et cetera; and from looking at the aerial photo and just what was in the vicinity targets, such as the railhead, the factory, et cetera, those are also military targets, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And the two you've just identified, the rail yard and the factory, I believe you have already indicated in your statements and exhibits that those are military targets. What I'm attempting to discover is whether the change of your opinion after your third statement is based on any new information or any information which is different from the information you had in your possession at the time you made your third statement.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: No, it was not. It was still just based on the information that I had from my original -- original statement of what was in the vicinity, such as the Ministry of Defence, the barracks, et cetera; and when you look at those, as well as the POL station and everything, those were strategic targets, and that was what made me think that the overall town of Knin was, in fact -- or, in fact, did have numerous military targets that could have made it a military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Are any of the facts upon which you base your in opinion --or let me just ask it this way: Are the facts upon which you're basing your new opinion in any way different than the facts upon which you based your original opinion that the shelling was indiscriminate?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: No there they're not, it's just that I changed my opinion from indiscriminate to unnecessary. The shelling still continued, there was collateral damage; however, there were military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could please refer to your journal, which is Exhibit P748; and in your tab, this appears at tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in P748, if we could go to page 15, which is the entry for 31 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in that entry for 31 August 1995, you state: "Colonel Leslie, now UNCRO COS, called Lieutenant-Colonel Tymchuk and asked if I would be willing to do him a favour, even though it was illegal (no photo taking allowed) and possibly very dangerous." Can you explain to the Court what exactly was "illegal" about the favour Colonel Leslie asked you to do on that date?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: The terminology of "illegal," in my opinion, it was not an illegal order given by the general at the time. The order was fine and I would have done it, and I had no problem in obeying that order. What was illegal was the taking of photos or the order not to take photos given to us by both the Sers prior to the offensive and then the Croats after the offensive took place. That was the illegal portion of it. It was not the order that was given to me by General Leslie through Colonel Tymchuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Okay. I think I'm a bit confused by your answer. You say that what was illegal was the taking of photos or the ordering not to take photos given to us by the Serbs. That seems to be a bit different than your entry. Your entry saying that the favour that General Leslie asked to you do was illegal?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That is not true. That is not an accurate statement because the -- the order was not illegal. It -- what was illegal was, in the opinion of the Croats, was taking photos. It was not the order that General Leslie gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And can I understand that to mean that you believed it was illegal to take photos?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: If you use the terminology "illegal" in the sense of disobeying the Croats, the answer was, yes, on that one, it was illegal. But was it illegal to take photos? Was it an illegal order by the General? The answer was no. I was responding to a direct order from a colonel at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And staying in that same entry, pardon me, you indicate that Colonel Leslie asked to you look for evidence that the HV/HVO had committed war crimes by indiscriminately shelling the city, and you stated: "Master Bombardier Parlee and I found the evidence that Colonel Leslie was looking for big time." Can you tell the Court what "big time" evidence was that you found?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: The "big time" refers to the number of buildings or craters, shrapnel, in various cars, buildings, windows, broken windows, et cetera. That is what I meant by "big time." To me, seeing destruction, as was throughout the sector, was a lot, so that is why I put "big time." Once again, I will go back to my personal journal and say those were my own personal notes; and to me, it looked big time at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move back to your first statement at page 4. First statement is it P739; that is the first one in your tab. So P739, at page 4, and it's the third paragraph from the bottom, in which you discuss acts of deliberate destruction witnessed by you in several areas around Sector South. In the last sentence of that paragraph, you state: "Major Juric tried to explain it in the same way as Cermak; however, he was also telling Captain Hill and myself that they had to make sure that the Chetniks would not return." Also, in the following paragraph, you stated: "Major Juric told me and Captain Hill during one of our meetings following Operation Storm that it was his responsibility to clean up the area and to ensure that the Chetniks would not be able to come back to the area." Can you tell the Court whether Major Juric ever indicated to you exactly who he considered Chetniks to be?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: It wasn't only Major Juric, but Major Juric in particular indicated that the Chetniks were the Serbs. He did not distinguish between Serbs civilians or Serb soldiers or Serb children or anything. A Chetnik was a Serb, in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And when -- what exactly was Major Juric explaining when he said that they had no make sure the Chetniks would not return? What was it he was attempting to go explain to you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I remember the incident quite well. It was up in the area of Macure, when Kistanje was ablaze. He -- he had stopped us and asked what we were doing in the area. We said we were just looking at what was happening throughout the sector, trying to ascertain what activities were still ongoing. We told Major Juric that we noticed there was a number of buildings that were on fire or destroyed after the offensive itself. That is when Major Juric indicated to us that we -- that the purpose of the operation was to clear the area of any -- "Chetniks" in the area had to be cleared out because they did not want them to come back and reoccupy areas of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one clarifying question? You used during your last answer the word "reoccupy." Did you mean reoccupy in a military sense or in the sense of, again, living in that area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a combination of both, Your Honour, both the civilians reoccupying the residence or the military coming back into their former positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berikoff. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be you who is the first to cross-examines Mr. Berikoff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I just gather my information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Berikoff, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Captain.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Consistent with our conversation yesterday, we will go through a series of matters, and pardon me if I just go through some things and jump around a little bit, but we will cover some matters that were covered on direct, as well as covering some matters that are just contain the in your statement but were not addressed. Okay?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, again, if you're not clear about any question, Captain, please stop me and just ask?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: If I may just ask one thing, Mr. Kehoe, may I be referred to as Mr. Berikoff. My military days are long gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. Berikoff.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I invite both speakers not to speak too quickly and also to make a short break between question and answer and answer and question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, prior to coming to the former Yugoslavia, even coming into Zagreb, you told us on direct examination that you were part of the Yugoslav crisis cell back in the nationality defence headquarters in Ottawa. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how long did you do that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: From April 1991 until April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you were followed -- I'm sorry. So you were following the sequence of events in Yugoslavia even prior to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let's go directly to your arrival, and if I could go to 748, your daily journal.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: What date is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The 21st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me just cover a couple of matters that -- it will be the 21st of July, the 22nd of July. And if I could just reference those, and then I did ask you a few questions about it. In the 21st of July, you note that you are flying over the area coming into Knin, and you note about halfway down that a lot of places are destroyed. Do you see that, sir, about one, two --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this is the -- this area was the area that was controlled by the Serbs at the time, right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we go down to the 22nd of July, about midway through, you note: "As I drive through the villages, it is it hard to imagine what these people have done to each other supposedly in the name of religion. One village will be destroyed and deserted, while the village next to it doesn't get touched."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, again, sir, this was -- these were Croatian villages that had been destroyed by the Serbs after 1991. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And a little bit more description. I mean, tell us the level of that damage, sir, the damage that was done by the Serbs against the Croats.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: A lot of the damage done was very similar to the damage that was done following the -- or during and following the offensive during Operation Storm. There were villages that were completely destroyed, there were villages that were partially destroyed, but the type of damage was very similar -- similar that took place during Operation Storm, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, even prior to Storm, you and the other UN personnel saw that all these Croatian villages had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes. It was very obvious that the destruction had taken place some time prior to August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, when you're talking about Croatian villages, could you please always make clear whether we're talking about villages in Croatia, which are Croatian villages --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and villages which are predominantly inhabited by those of Croatian ethnic origin, so that we have a clear designation between what is a Croatian village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, perhaps, we could ask Mr. Berikoff the last questions about the damage to the villages, the question always was about Croatian villages. In your answers, when you confirmed what was put to you by Mr. Kehoe, did you include that the damage was done to villages of a predominantly Croatian population, or were you just talking about villages you saw in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was villages both on Croatian -- in Croatia proper and, once again, Croatian dominantly populated villages in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you noted that these -- this was the similar type damage that you saw after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know when you -- prior to Operation Storm if the United Nations was making any efforts with the RSK authorities to determine who did all this burning of Croat houses?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I had heard rumours of that, but I'm not aware of anything in particular, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your were aware that a large number of Croatian civilians had been driven out.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you got to Sector South, would you agree that -- that the whole area of the Krajina was very tense?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Without a doubt. There were indications and rumours and conflicting stories of a possible Croatian offensive to retake the Krajina. There were ongoing negotiations about the status of the Krajina. And the days varied from -- well, we may have an offensive starting tomorrow, we may have an offensive in ten days, a week, whatever. So, yes, it was a very stressful situation throughout. Even prior to my deployment, even while I was in Canada at the nationality defence headquarters, I was still aware of the possibility of an upcoming offensive against the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in your diary -- I'm just -- there was also a problem with the Krajina Serbs conducting criminal activities against the United Nations as well. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes. There were a number of instances when United Nations vehicles were hijacked. In one instance prior to my arrival, one of the UN personnel was shot during -- shot and killed during a hijacking; and yes, this was done by the local Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, by way of clarity, Your Honour, this is -- I believe Mr. Berikoff is on the bottom of page 2 on to page 3 of P748.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in addition to that, sir, if I may, and just trying to get your statements together. When you got there, sir, there was also a significant degree of restriction of movement, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Throughout the whole -- whole area, we were restricted at a number of check-points of being able to go any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the restrictions were by the ARSK, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that began towards the latter part of July of 1995, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, it did, that I'm aware of. It may have happened before, but definitely when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when you got there, Mr. Berikoff, the ARSK, at least in your experience, began to refuse your entry into certain areas. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, they did, or they let us in after we waited a certain amount of time; or if we were able to pay them certain items such as Coca-Cola or cigarettes, then they would let us through. So the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the areas they were moving in to, were they moving troops and other mechanized vehicles?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: It was usually in areas where there was military activity, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And where would that have been?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly; however, I do know that it was on the way to -- from Knin down south towards Drnis in that area. I don't recall the exact areas. We also went to other areas where we were restricted at various check-points throughout the whole sector, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But to follow up on what you said before, you learned during this period of time that these restrictions were taking place because they were moving troops and mechanized vehicles.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: In a lot of the cases, it was because of troop or vehicle movement. Whether it was mechanized or not, sir, I'm not sure, but it was vehicle movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now you note for news your diary, again, at -- if I may, on the 1st of August, that you were supposed to take a helicopter recce along the zone of separation to visit CanBat 1's area of responsibility. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And it was it wasn't only the CanBat's 1's area of responsibility, it was the whole zone of separation, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell us, and tell the Chamber, what you were intending to do with the recce.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Basically, what the reconnaissance would do would give -- provides us with information about troop movement, troop locations, et cetera, on both sides of the warring factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you tried to take this reconnaissance flight on the 1st of August, the ARSK refused, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did they give you a reason why they refused?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you attempted to take that reconnaissance flight again the next day, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that would have been 2 August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, take that reconnaissance mission?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: It was either the 2nd or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Or did you take it thereafter?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: It was on the 2nd of August, as you indicated. That's when the pilot picked me up at the UN compound on our helipad. We departed at 8.00. At 8.08, I believe, is when we got fired upon by the ARSK from the area of Oklaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So they refused permission on the 1st; you got fired upon; and going back to your diary, on the 3rd, your reconnaissance mission - and I'm talking about your diary, P748, on the 3rd of August - your reconnaissance mission on that day was, once again, refused by the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Because after the incident and after the apology from the ARSK colonel, we had put in another request for permission to fly again the next day; however, that mission was cancelled completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, did the -- did you learn during this period of time when you were being denied this movement, Mr. Berikoff, that the ARSK was preparing an offensive against the HV?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: No, I did not. We were denied numerous attempts of doing many things by the ARSK in the early days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Such as what else, sir?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Such as entry into areas along some of my travels. My task, when I was there, was to gain information. So on numerous occasions, I would drive to various locations throughout the sector and was denied entry into various areas, not necessarily just military. If there was a civilian police check-point, I would be turned around and told I could not go into the area. No reason was given; however, there were numerous incidents when we were turned, and permission was not given for us to go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I earlier did not know whether it was important enough to take the witness back to page 68, lines 16 and following; but in view of your line of questioning, I think it might have gained some importance. Mr. Berikoff, you were asked about the restrictions of movement, and one of the questions put to you: "And that began towards the latter part of July of 1995, didn't it?" You said: "Yes, it did, that I'm aware of. It may have happened before, but definitely when I was there." Then the next question was: "So when you got there, Mr. Berikoff, the ARSK, at least in your experience, began to refuse your entry into certain areas; isn't that right?" And you said: "Yes, they did." Now, the whole of the context leaves some doubt as to whether what you noticed upon arrival was something that began - that is, that they began to restrict freedom of movement - or whether you say, I experienced that there was freedom of movement, and I do not know whether it began at that time or before I arrived. Could you please clarify this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could, Your Honour. There was restriction of movement and even before I got there. The restriction of movement was in effect. There were hijackings, there was everything, so there restrictions of movement imposed by ARSK, as well as some restriction of movement imposed by the UN command within Sector South itself, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe, the first answer of the witness already hinted quite clearly at whether it began at the time he arrived that that might not have been the case. You more or less ignored that answer. In introducing the next question, when saying that: "When you got there, they began to refuse." Apart from the -- well, of course, in your experience, but I noticed that. But if you haven't been there before, you can't have any experience. And from the explanation of the witness now, it appears that he had knowledge of what happened before he arrived, and he noticed that when he was there, that there was restriction of movement. And in the beginning, I think it would have assisted the Chamber better if would you not have, again, used that word "began to refuse." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I think using the words "ongoing restriction of movement" might explain it easier. I was ongoing when I got there. I was aware that there was restriction of movement prior to my arrival; and when I got there, the restriction of movement was ongoing, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You experienced that it was there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could be a little bit more precise on that, Mr. Berikoff, and I can turn your attention to P740, paragraph 2-A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, I might explain to Mr. Berikoff who might not be familiar with the Dutch testing system of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- our alarm sirens. That is what happened every Monday, first of the month at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As everyone in the courtroom blithely ignores.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Hopefully, nothing will happen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know if -- -

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... at noontime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is P740, if we can bring that up on the screen, paragraph 2-A.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Perhaps I should have clarified this for you prior to my questioning. It notes that: "Prior to Operation Storm on 27 July, while returning from Primosten to Knin, ARSK soldiers stopped everybody at their check-points. There was no UN vehicle movement allowed into areas that we had previously been permitted."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And the stoppage of going into these areas was being done by the ARSK, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And they were stopping you - not you - they were stopping UN personnel from going into areas that UN personnel had previously gone to.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you began to -- well, you put this in your -- your statement, so I take it that that was an indicator to you that things were changing?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were changing substantially, in that there was very different types of activity throughout area, in particular with the ARSK either through the -- through the means of call-up or whatever. We were stopped on numerous occasions and not allowed to go into areas as indicated in my report, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in addition to that, sir, there was also some dissatisfaction with the ARSK personally, as you reflect in paragraph 2-C of this document, that the ARSK, in fact, put you on a hit list. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think you explain it in a little bit more detail in your diary, P748, which is the entry for the 30th of July, if you can go to that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go to P748, next page. It's the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of that entry on the 30th, it notes the area about the hit list and the black market ring. Tell us a little bit about that what was going on?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Myself and Captain Dangerfield and his driver Sergeant Green made numerous visits to the observation post or OP up in Strmica. During one of our visits, the Kenyan platoon commander informed us that he had been told by a Serb police officer that, in fact, Captain Dangerfield and I were placed on a hit list. There was a contract out on both of us because there -- they accused of us passing information back to our UN headquarters regarding troop movement, et cetera. There was further -- he further stated to us that we were interfering with an ongoing trade agreement between the local ARSK and the observation post personnel themselves. And by us being there, we were infringing on their, I guess, extra circular activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what was this trade agreement between the UN personnel and the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: The ARSK allegedly were providing food rations, et cetera, and female company for the exchange of fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it was an exchange of prostitutes going to the UN in exchange for fuel?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That is one of the things that we were told, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And because you revealed that with Captain Dangerfield, you were put on this hit list?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes. Well, both Captain Dangerfield and I were told of this at the same time. I did not reveal it to Captain Dangerfield; he and I were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in addition to these other issues, there was also a degree of tension that arose because of the fact there was a general mobilisation at the latter part of July, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, it is. There was tension throughout the area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you became -- the gap in time, Mr. Berikoff, is to allow the translators to catch up.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: No problem, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you, yourself, began do travel to areas that were up near Bosnia, for instance, and Bosansko Grahovo that were the subject of that ongoing military activity for which this mobilisation was to support. Suspect; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now what did you observe coming back and forth, going in and outside of the Bosansko Grahovo area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: We observed a lot of military movement between the Krajina and up into the Bosansko Grahovo area, as well as military movement coming back: Types of vehicles included tank -- track vehicles, including tanks. There soft-skinned vehicles, ammunition carriers, troops, there were also ambulances taking casualties down the hill into the Serb area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you say "tanks," sir, what are you talking about and in what numbers?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I can't be specific, but it was -- a number of tanks were going back and forth. Whether it was the same tanks or whether it was additional tanks, I cannot answer that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just to put this in a time-frame, let us turn our attention which is 744, which is your time-line with Mr. Williams, and it notes the date of this Knin radio call as the 27th of July. Do you see that, sir? It's on the first page of P744, your Sector South --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that about right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That's about right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you were also aware, sir, that -- that the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Mr. Martic, noted that there was a state of war in the entire area of the RSK. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you got to Sector South headquarters, General Forand sent you down to find out what was going on, sent you to find out what happen being in the area, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, he did. When we got there, there was a bare map on the wall. He told me, he said, "Phil, I need information. I don't have anything on any of the warring factions." And he gave me a set of keys to an SUV, and it was my task to go out daily and virtually push the envelope to -- as far as I can, to see if I would encounter any troops on either side of -- either warring faction, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And pursuant to that, Mr. Berikoff, he sent you up to Strmica on the 30th of July.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, he did. There was a great deal of activity, artillery shelling, et cetera, up in the Bosansko Grahovo area. He sent myself -- myself, and I believe Captain Williams came with me, up there to spend the evening. I'm not sure if it was Williams or Dangerfield, but we spent the evening up in the Strmica area observing and just sort of listening to the amount of artillery that was going on, on the other side of the -- on the Bosnian side of the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, did you hear the artillery fire going back and forth?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Back and forth, yes. It was -- there was extensive artillery fire that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I can turn your attention back to your diary, P748, for the entry of the 30th of July, 1995. Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for it to come back up on the screen. The next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It should be the next page, page -- there we go. The 30th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you read that for us, about four lines down, it begins with the sentence: "It was very interesting ..." Do you see that, Mr. Berikoff?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "It was very interesting, and I was able to see all kinds of equipment on the way. This includes BMPs, M-12 anti-tank guns, M-84 tanks, and a lot of other pieces of kit I don't recognise."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What is that stuff?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: The M-12, it is an anti-tank gun. It fires armour-piercing shells. The M-84 is a more modern Yugoslav-type tank. That are those two, and the BMP is an armoured personnel carrier, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I think we missed the entry for what the M-12 is. What is the M-12?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: It is an anti-tank gun. It fires armour-piercing rounds or high explosives, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You not there that, two lines down, there are -- many RSK are around the area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was an ARSK camp down about an a thousand metres from the Kenyan outpost.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And say there are many RSK around. How many did you observe?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I observed at least a company strength in that area at various times. There was always sentries on duty, there was different types of vehicles in the compound, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, these tanks and BMPs and other items, did you notice them on the move?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise. I don't mean to cut counsel off. Your Honour, I believe at page 79, here at line -- I'm sorry. It has just been corrected. It was first "canyon" outpost. It has been corrected now to "Kenyan" outpost. I just wanted to make sure that correction was been made at line 3. It has been. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, did you notice these vehicles on the move?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You indicated you were up there on the 30th of July?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, we did. In fact, on numerous occasions that we were in the area of Strmica, there was vehicle movement from that compound up over the border into the Bosansko Grahovo area. I assume that it was in the Bosansko Grahovo area. But, yes, there was vehicle movement quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And where was the ARSK moving this equipment from?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where the ARSK was moving the equipment from, but some of it, I assume, would have come from the compound or garrison a thousand metres from where the Kenyan observation post was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you familiar, Mr. Berikoff, with the ARSK ammunition depot at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I am not familiar -- I know it was there. That is my familiarity with it. I don't what was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how do you know it was there?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Because it was information that I was given, that's all, prior to my arrival in the Knin area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with this mobilisation that you learned and with -- With this mobilisation that you were aware of and with the vehicle movement and number of troops up in Strmica, was it your belief at that time, Mr. Berikoff, that that the ARSK was moving their personnel towards the front line?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: At the time, it was my impression that ARSK members were going across the border to assist with the operation in the Bosansko Grahovo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, just trying to be a bit more specific here, Mr. Berikoff, were they moving their troops towards what was a front line area with the HV?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I would have to say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, just going back to your -- your supplemental sheet that you provided -- that was provided us, while you were up in Strmica, you did not observe any shelling of HV of residential areas, did you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: No. I did not observe direct evidence of shelling in the Strmica area; however, there were indications of buildings destroyed and they were recent -- it was recent destruction, rather than -- than pre-offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this recent destruction, did it appear to be part of this artillery barrage that was going back and forth?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: It could have been; however, I did not witness any shelling into the Strmica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying with this issue, if we can go back, you noted that were there on the 30th of July. If I can go back to your P744 which is your chronology that did you with Captain Williams, and if we can go to the second page of that document, we go to the entry for the 31st of July. Excuse me. It notes on the 31st of July : "118 artillery shells, 30 HV, 30 HVO; 88 ARSK were fired or impacted between the warring factions?" Is that right, WFS?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "ARSK appears to be reacting to the offense of Bosansko -- in Bosansko Grahovo by redeploying forces." Going down to the entry for the 2nd, there is another entry for artillery fire: "Between 10.30 and 13.58, HV, HVO fired 34 artillery rounds in the area of Strmica, between ..." --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: "Towards an unknown position in BiH."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "0430 to 0530, RSK fired 50 artillery rounds from the general area of Strmica to ward an unknown position in BiH." Suffice it say, Mr. Berikoff, there was a lot of activity going on --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me just finish. I'm just waiting for the --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Suffice it to say, Mr. Berikoff, there was a lot of activity going on -- military activity going on between the ARSK and the HV, HVO towards the latter part of July and the early part of August; wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, there was, and I'm not denying that. There was a lot of activity up in the Strmica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, sir, please understand I'm not challenging what you're saying, just clarifying a few issues here.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, during this period of time, and I direct your attention to your supplemental information sheet, you told the Prosecutor that you personally observed "people leaving Knin prior to Operation Storm and recalls that it was a significant number of people that left." If I can turn your attention to your 21 May 1997 statement at paragraph 2-B, that's P270 -- excuse me, P740. You note as of the -- on "B": "On 29 July, many of the UN civilian employees did not show up for work. We later found out that they had started to evacuate from the area because they were afraid of a Croat offensive in the Krajina at a near future" -- excuse me, "in the very near future." So based on your observations, Mr. Berikoff, the departure of civilians or the evacuation of civilians took place some five, six days before Operation Storm even took place. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, it does. Because as I indicated earlier, we weren't certain of when a possible offensive would start. We were given information anything from one day to ten days. I'm sure the civilian population would have had the same type of information. On that day in particular, we were placed on Orange Alert because of additional information through various means that we received. So it's -- it is quite possible that, yes, they did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So based -- if I may -- based on your observations, Mr. Berikoff, as early as the 29th of July, civilians were leaving on their own?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me address some of your observations concerning the actual military situation in the Krajina as -- and Knin, as well as the shelling. Now, the first is that -- and you said this in direct examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, are we moving to another subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps, looking at the clock, it would be better to have a break now and resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, I was go to go on to a new topic now that deals with actual shelling of Knin on the 4th of August. I think you told us that on direct that you did changed your opinion on the indiscriminate nature of the shelling. Did I hear you correctly that that change of opinion took place sometime in 1997 or 1998?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That's correct. It was -- in addition, it was on my mind immediately after the offensive and over a period of time, yes, it did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we talk about Knin directly, Mr. Berikoff, I want to draw a little bit on your experience in the military, and especially the JNA and Warsaw Pact nations' methodologies. You are familiar with those based or your experience, are you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you do know that within the JNA, the structure of the military is very much a top-down type of enterprise, where the lower level soldiers and units don't do anything without an order from the top. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That's correct. It very similar to the -- as in all former Warsaw Pact counties, the chain of command, the structure was very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that's quite different than the approach taken by NATO countries, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: In the sense that in NATO countries, everybody from the top down, for instance, can read a map. Everybody knows what the operation is, what the objective of an operation is normally, and the sequence of events that will follow, following an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that among the NATO philosophy that if there is a destruction of communication and command and control operations at a high level, that lower level entities or elements can essentially think for themselves?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: In most cases, I would have to agree with you. There are those instances where information may not have been passed down; but, yes, in general terms, I would totally agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you knew that Operation Storm was -- had taken place not only in Sector South but also the in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it was a broad range of -- or broad area of geography, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as a military person, Mr. Berikoff, if you were to disrupt the structure of the ARSK, you would strike at their headquarters and their communication networks, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: In particular the communication, yes. However, with regard to communications, the one thing that the former Warsaw pact countries did have which was very, very good in comparison to NATO-type countries was the redundancy of communications. So there may have been a redundancy of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But, in any event, if you were planning the operation, you would, first and foremost, attempt to destroy a headquarters and the communications because that would affect the operations, not only in Sector South in Knin but throughout the Krajina. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I would have to agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't mean to interrupt. It is just unclear to me if he is being asked if he would do that or if he is being asked, if you were a Warsaw member nation, would do you that -- or former Warsaw Pact nation, would you do that. I'm not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood the question to be what the witness would do if he would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's how it was phrased, Mr. Russo. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By the way, what was the "redundancy of communications" mean?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: It means that they have extra capabilities that they would not lose communications at any given time; that if one communications system was destroyed or made inoperable, there was another system that would take over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So a wise military commander that wanted to destroy the communication network would, in fact, attempt to target all communication networks because of this redundancy issue. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That would be the ideal situation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that would come in conjunction with attempting to take out the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, it would, normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let me direct your attention to D117, and this is a NATO glossary of terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we could move to the second page of that, and if we could move towards the bottom of that page and blow up the centre column last entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And we're talking about NATO'S discussion of the centre of gravity, characteristics, capabilities, or localities, from which a nation and alliance on military force or other grouping derives its freedom of action, physical strength, or will to fight. Now, Mr. Berikoff, that is Knin, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: At that point in time, the answer is yes. It was their main or one of their main headquarters, it had a garrison, it had other barracks, et cetera. So, yes, it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, again, if you were a military commander, you would do everything in your power to talk out - you mentioned the communication, the headquarters - but anything that was supporting that structure as well, wouldn't you.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: If you knew where the locations were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if I may -- oops. When you were in -- well, let me direct your attention to page 9 of D284.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can go page 9 of to 284, line 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You note in this that: "In my opinion, the type of ammunition that was used for the offensive against Knin was ... a high explosive variety mainly used for destruction of buildings and facilities." So you would agree, Mr. Berikoff, that as a commanding officer, if you were to take out these buildings which housed communication facilities, you would use weaponry such as that used by the HV, that was designed for the destruction of buildings and facilities, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, in the destruction of the buildings and facilities, based on your statement herein, the HV used the right type of ammunition, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, they did. For the targets intended, if that was their intention, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, your issue is the number of shells involved, and that's your question, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the information concerning the number of shells, you received that information from Colonel -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be some kind of interference which has now stopped again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge. Am I okay to go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now the number of shells is information you received from Colonel Leslie, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
