utterances.text: It was both Colonel Leslie and Master Bombardier Parlee who were both artillery personnel and had knowledge of how to count the rounds. As a military officer, I also had the basic knowledge of artillery shelling from flash-to-bang counting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Since your time in the former Yugoslavia, and I include both your time in Knin and Sarajevo, have you spoken to Colonel Leslie?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: No, I have not, sir, at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you learn either directly or indirectly that he has stated that these shell counts were not accurate?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: No. I am not aware what General Leslie has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, we note the level of shelling that was going on. And if I could just take you through some of the items that you have presented to us to just discuss a little bit, the shelling and number of shells that you maintain was improper given the fact that the -- you say the ARSK had vacated the area. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That issue, of course, has nothing to do with taking out the communications network, does it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: No, it would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we can go to P744, which, again, is your chronology with Captain Williams.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that is my chronology with Captain Williams, sir. I would say I had input in some of the information that was given. He. Captain Williams, received information from a variety and a multitude of sources to put that document together. I only provided bits and pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand. But let us, nonetheless, go through some of those entries, and let's turn to page 3 of this document. We're talking about the evening of the 4th of August. Now, if you look at the entry for 1715, which is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, down on the 4th, there were reporting that start: "Much of the reporting ..." This comes from the ARSK: "Much of the reporting speaks of repelling the HV." Now, throughout the 4th, there was significant fighting going on with the HV and the -- and the ARSK, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I would not disagree with that, because if the intention of the Croats was to take the Krajina, there would be fighting throughout the Krajina, not just in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you noted for us during the course of your direct examination that you had spent quite a bit of time with Captain Dangerfield?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Captain Dangerfield was another British officer attached to UN Sector South.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was a liaison officer from Gornji Vakuf in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to his report, which is P698, if we may. What I'd like to do, Mr. Berikoff, is go through a few of these excerpts here, as opposed to go through one by one, and allow you to speak about them just a bit. And this is a brief overview from Sector South on the 4th of August at 0500 to 2200 on the August [sic], and Captain Dangerfield gives some information about the shelling. He notes in paragraph 2: "It was a long time before the HVO," excuse me, "HV/HVO made any headway on the ground. In the early afternoon, the picture began to develop as soon as we saw five main areas of attack." And he discusses those particular areas in paragraph 3, and notes: "By mid afternoon, five main axis of attack had developed."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is his assessment for the 5th of August : "Saturday, 05 August, should see another -- should see another initial heavy artillery barrage of HV objectives. G2 assessment ..." That is you, is it not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: No, it's not. That is probably the G2 from UNCRO or the G2 from Gornji Vakuf who he answered to. Captain Dangerfield didn't not respond to UNCRO headquarters; he normally responded to the operational side or to Gornji Vakuf, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Fair enough. "G2 assessment is that Knin may fall dark, 05 August. In order to do, I believe that the HV will require a more successful day than today." Now, Mr. Berikoff, was it your assessment, consistent with Mr. Dangerfield, that the ARSK was putting up a pretty good fight against the HV throughout the 4th?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: In certain areas of the sector, yes, there was, heavy fighting to medium amount of fighting, but, yes, there was fighting throughout the sector, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the answer to my question that the ARSK was putting up a pretty significant fight, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: The answer is yes, at times they were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Continuing on. "Troops approaching from the south face stiff opposition. SLO recces, last week, saw consider use of road use by ARSK track vehicles." Now, were you aware of these ARSK track vehicles moving into areas in the southern part of the sector?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: In the southern part of the sector, yes. Not so much that it was track vehicles; however, there was military movement. As I said to you earlier on, we -- there was a further restriction of movement down in the area from Drnis to Knin. So there was military movement. Whether it was track movement, I'm not sure, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you talk -- I'm sorry. Did you talk to Mr. Dangerfield about -- I'm sorry. Did you talk to Captain Dangerfield about these track vehicles, ARSK track vehicles, moving in the south part of the sector?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I don't recall specifically talking to Captain Dangerfield regarding the tank vehicles. A lot of the information that Captain Dangerfield received was through the operations who got reports from all the various parts of the sector. So, although I spoke regularly with certain topics to Captain Dangerfield, I don't recall specifically talking about the track vehicles. We did speak about military movement, movement of personnel, movement of BMPs. If you call a BMP a track vehicle versus a tank, then the answer is, yes, to that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Captain Dangerfield is the officer that you were travelling around the sector with quite frequently prior to Operation Storm, is he not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, he is. And, again, on a few occasions following the operation as well, I was with Captain Dangerfield; but prior to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Going down to the next paragraph, 11: "In the west, HV advances face problems of indirect major routes, and at times difficult terrain in approaches towards Knin. With reports being unclear on the successes of these axis of advance and the distance still required to cover, it is unlikely that Knin will come under direct fire from them."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: What's the question, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, both the terrain and -- was it both the terrain and the existence of a significant force of the ARSK in the west that the UN believed that the -- that the HV was not going to be able to make it down into Knin, or, certainly, as this item notes, that Knin was not going to come under direct fire from them? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That's quite possible because there were ARSK strongholds in Oklaj and areas. So there may have been areas where there were buildup of ARSK troops. The terrain, as Captain Dangerfield indicates, was not conducive to a wide area of movement by armoured vehicles, so they would be restricted. There were also a lot of land-mines throughout the sector. That would restrict movement. So, yes, his assessment is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page, paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Paragraph 12: "While Knin may come under heavy artillery attack again, the considerable presence of the ARSK forces in the area will require more time before they come under direct fire from HV tanks." If we can just go down to paragraph 15, we'll deal with this together. "The request for aid to evacuate women and children, leaving behind ARSK troops only, shows signs of a disturbing final showdown. With the advancing HV/HVO troops looking at Knin as their final objective, and ARSK troops remaining, Milan Martic will have to surrender or face a bloody last stand in the capital of Krajina." Now, before I ask you something about this, I'd like to show you something else, which is a transcript of a radio intercept. And it is D106 of ARSK General Mrksic on the evening of the 4th of August, 1995, at 2130 hours. About midway down in this Radio Belgrade conversation with General Mrksic, it reads: "Q. Does that mean our lines have been penetrated? "A. No. We are maintaining contact. Our forces withdrew to the positions for direct defence of Knin. The other range units are still successfully holding their positions."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can stroll down that page just a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: About three-fifths of the way down, it says, "If the VRS ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "If the VRS, army of Republika Srpska, succeeds in putting the pressure on the forces attacking in the direction of Grahovo-Knin, we shall then stabilize the defence and switch to a counterattack." Lastly, if I could just read to you, this was an audio presentation, Mr. Berikoff, by Colonel Leslie on the evening of the 4th of August, at 2340, CET: "In your judgement ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By the way, this is D123. Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The reporter asks: "In your judgement, are the Croats on the point of taking the town?" Leslie: "Taking Knin, no. We had no reports of Croatians being within direct fire range of Knin, and there's still a lot of Serbs in Knin and in the surrounding hills. So there we go." Now, Mr. Berikoff, at this particular point, the assessment of the UN is that the ARSK is going to retreat into Knin, and, as Captain Dangerfield said, either surrender or face a bloody last stand. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I wouldn't totally agree with Captain Dangerfield's assessment. In my journal, I had indicated that there were ARSK forces; and, in all likelihood, they had moved up to defence lines to protect the city of Knin. I wouldn't go as far as when he said there was strong opposition. It was in certain areas where there was opposition, but not throughout the sector. But, generally, I would agree with his assessment, but not totally, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you're familiar, Mr. Berikoff, of street fighting in and around a city, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I am. It is one of the most complicated and difficult operations to conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it is very costly when it comes to personnel, too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, it is. One person can stop a whole platoon or company, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, do you agree that on the evening of the 4th, consistent with Colonel Leslie's comments, that Knin was not on the verge of falling?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Not at that time, no. However, there were no troops right in the town itself either or very minimal. But was it on the verge of falling that evening? The answer is no to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Am I okay, Judge? I'm just trying to make sure that I'm not getting ahead of the translators, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As we move into the 5th, the UN observed a series of troop and mechanized elements moving in the Sector South area towards Knin, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, they did, as indicated by Captain Dangerfield in his report. I generally agree with that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me show you a sitrep, specifically D124. This is a sitrep, an UNMO sitrep, on the 5th of August at 1900.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go that page, number 3, "CanBat."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is it at 0535. It notes: "RSK movement of tanks and vehicles," and it notes in the following paragraph that the vehicles seen headed towards Knin. As we move back down that page, you can see the second-to-last note saying that they're headed towards Knin. If go towards the next page, it likewise notes in the first two entries that they are headed towards Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can bring up on the screen 65 ter 1634.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This sitrep, Mr. Berikoff, of CanBat at 0800 Zulu on 5 August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is began a CanBat update.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we go down towards the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As you can see, it is talking about ARSK elements. And 4, at 0530 vehicles heading towards Knin, six T-54s and six T-34s and one BRDM.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can offer this up into evidence at this time, 65 ter 1634.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D727, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D727 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying with P744, that's, again, the chronology with Mr. Williams -- excuse me, on page 3. At 6.10 a.m. on the 5th, it notes: "Eight ARSK tanks, one BOV." What is a BOV, sir.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: It's a -- APC is an armoured personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "One BOV, one truck, heading from the south to north through Knin." So if can we can just set the stage for these questions, Mr. Berikoff, we have a significant amount of fighting going on through the 4th; the lines haven't been penetrated; General Mrksic says that they are preparing a defence of Knin; troop personnel and mechanised units are heading towards Knin; you, in fact, see or UN observes tanks moving through Knin in the earlier morning hours of the 5th. Under those circumstances, is it reasonable for a commander to believe that there's going to be ongoing fighting in Knin throughout the 5th?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Not necessarily. Knin -- the troop ARSK troops that moved out of Knin went to the forward deployment area. So would there be fighting in Knin? Quite possibly not. In the area of Knin? Yes. Up in the forward line? Yes, quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You note here that there are tanks moving through Knin?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. And is it reasonable for a commander to fire on those tanks as they move through Knin?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: If they were observed and the opportunity arose, yes, it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if, in fact, a defence is going to take place, as General Mrksic outlined, is it reasonable for a commander to continue to fire on headquarters and communication facilities that were going to be used to support that defence of Knin?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I don't mean to interrupt the flow, and I'm certainly not objecting to the line of questioning. I just want to be clear. This has come up several times, the Defence has made a motion about fact witnesses offering opinions regarding this. I'm not suggesting that you shouldn't be doing it, but I just want to be clear that we're now putting hypothetical information to a fact witness and soliciting an opinion about whether or not it is reasonable for a commander to act in one set or another. I want to be to clear that if that is okay with the Defence, I just want to make sure that we're not still subject to the objection that made regarding this line of questioning to fact witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may respond. The Prosecution asked this witness about his assessment of shelling and whether or not it was excessively shelled, and that entails both the 4th as well as the 5th. That is an opinion that has been brought out by Mr. Russo. We are attempting to meet that opinion with the sequence of facts for Mr. Berikoff to take into consideration as to whether or not a reasonable commander can continue to fire when a commanding officer says that there's going to a defence of Knin, and that there has been continuous fighting throughout that day, and, at least the assessment of Mr. Dangerfield is, that there was a significant possibility of a bloody last stand in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, you did not raise an objection, so there we have a non-objection and we have an explanation. It seems to me that having heard quite a bit of evidence on that, it is not uncommon for both parties to elicit, especially in the field of military matters, to seek testimony which is not of a purely factual nature and even includes wise commanders, as I meanwhile understand. Let's move on. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Moving back to that question, Mr. Berikoff.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Under the circumstances of the 5th of August, when General Mrksic maintains that there is going to be a defence of Knin to take place, General Leslie says that Croat lines have not been penetrated, and that there is ARSK movement towards Knin, and there's no evidence that the communication network is - I meant the Serb lines haven't been penetrated - no evidence that the communication network per General Mrksic has been taken out, is it reasonable for a commander to again engage in artillery attack to take those elements out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to be clear that Mr. Berikoff is being asked to assume the accuracy of the facts upon which he is now being asked to offer an opinion. He has been shown evidence. There is no indication -- well, he certainly has not been asked whether he is aware of this evidence, whether he agrees with it in particular, but I just want it be clear that the question is asking him to assume the accuracy of the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's, of course, always the problem with questions about opinion, that on what is the opinion based. Again, I repeat, that this is it not uncommon in the examination of both parties; and by highlighting it, Mr. Russo, you may have emphasised also that, of course, questions of fact do more assist the Chamber than to elicit too much opinion. At the same time, although it should be kept to a minimum --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- some assessment of what is useful, wise, effective, I'm afraid that we can't get totally rid of it, although the Chamber certainly would encourage you to get rid of it as much as possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, do you recall my question?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Even if the assessment and the reports are accurate, I think it is a commander's responsibility to take into consideration the possibility of collateral damage that may be caused by any firing upon any mean, whether they're travelling through a town or whether they were deployed into the area of the town itself. But, yes, if there is an opportunity to take out the troops while they're in movement, I would say yes, taking into considerations all or facts and based on the accuracy and inaccuracy of the report itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And your answer would include efforts to take out any communication facilities?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I would have to an I agree that one of the goals and objectives is the infrastructure of the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. Berikoff, were you aware that on the evening of the 4th of August, that General Mrksic put troops and artillery on the hill outside of Knin known as Bulina Strana? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: No, I am not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let us talk a little bit about some of your items that you put into evidence and some of the charts that you put into evidence. You did talk in your -- I believe your 2007 statement, which is P741, at paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If could you pull that up for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the middle part of that page, you talk about -- you see the shelling damage in this area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's extensive, and it came from both convention artillery and multi-barrel rocket launchers. Again, at paragraph 4 -- I'm sorry. Again paragraph 4, you note that: "There were multi-barrel rocket launcher impacts in residential areas between the hospital and downtown Knin, which is not in the vicinity of any military targets." Now, Mr. Berikoff, I think in our conversation yesterday you said that you didn't hear any shelling after 12.00 on the 5th. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that was shortly before the HV units came to your gate, the Sector South gate. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you do know that both the ARSK and the HV had multi-barrel rocket launcher systems. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, they did. It's a weapon similar to both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the shelling that you heard in and around Knin on -- didn't happen after noon, you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can go to P744, and if we can go to the entry for 10.00 on page 4 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At 10.00 on the 5th, it notes: "10.00 on 5 August, HV reportedly entered the city." If I can just address you to an item that the Prosecution has put into evidence. Which is the statement of a Mira Grubor, P54, she notes that: "Around 10.30 on Saturday morning, some shooting was heard at the entrance of the hospital. I saw a group of Croatian soldiers." So if the HV came into town on the 10th and you didn't hear shelling in Knin after noon -- I'm sorry. If the HV came into town on 1000 hours on the 5th, or thereabouts, and you didn't hear shelling after noontime, there was shelling going on in Knin when the HV was moving in, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you were aware that the ARSK was moving through the area and going back up into Strmica on the 5th. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you were -- are aware, as a military person, of an army protecting its rear by putting elements in their rear, to fire on to any oncoming soldiers, any oncoming enemy. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: As a rear echelon, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And often -- often, a rear echelon will use mortars because they're so mobile. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: The use of mortars is normally as an area weapon vice [sic] a direct impact area; but if, in fact, they are firing upon troop movement and stuff, they will use mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to the aerial that you talked about; and, if I may, it was aerial map that you had put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe it is it P746.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Bear with me, Mr. Berikoff, because I know this is difficult to see. Let us take, for instance, the area up by the hospital, and you see that circled with blue. I can't see the letter; it may be C? Is it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I know the area you're talking about, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe it is a "Q."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Oh, Mr. Misetic, says it is "F" ; you say it is "Q."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are talking about the blue circled area, which is just underneath the word "hospital" on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's right. That area, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you know that the hospital had not been shelled. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: It's my impression that -- or my further assessment was the hospital itself was not targeted. If any damage was done, it was probably done through collateral damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you do know that, as we look at this photograph, the Dinara mountains are off to the -- where? Would it be the east of the city?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: East of the city, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the HV came down those hills.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That was one of the axis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, as a retreating force, you know, Mr. Berikoff, that it would have been perfectly reasonable for the ARSK to fire on the HV troops as they moved into Knin. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: It would have been logical, but I don't recall if they did or not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you don't recall because, on the 5th, you were still back in Sector South headquarters and didn't have the opportunity to go out and see what was going on, right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: That's correct. I was busy tasked doing other things on the morning of the 5th; and then once the HV came to the gate, movement was restricted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you told us, Mr. Berikoff, that you saw evidence of shells in that location, and I'm talking about that area in blue right below the hospital, you have no idea when that took place, do you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: The actual impacts, no. However, during the actual offensive on the 4th and the artillery was coming in, there were artillery impacts and rocket impacts throughout the field. So if some landed by the hospital, they may have been that. But, yes, you're correct, some of it may have been caused by other forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you have no idea when you went back to that field which was caused by the HV and which was caused by the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: I have to agree with you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In fact, let us turn our attention to P60. P60 is a joint statement by two UNMOs, Tor Munkelien and Kari Anttila?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can go to the third page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is a discussion where on the 17th - you can read it Mr. Berikoff - Mr. Munkelien and Mr. Anttila retrieved a piece of an M-63, 128-millimetre MRL, which had been fired from approximately 20 degrees north by northeast. I will let you finish with that, sir.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: No problem. I have read the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can go to D88, taking the degrees of impact, sir, from north by north-east, as you can see from this map, and the angle. And they did a crater analysis upon this. As reflected in that report, it was fired from the direction 20 degrees north by north-east into an area of Strmica. Now, you know, sir, that Strmica was controlled on the 4th and the 5th and thereafter by the ARSK, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Are you saying on the 4th and 5th, it was still under ARSK control?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it remained in ARSK control until approximately when?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Berikoff, it is visible that you're consulting your notes. Would you please always indicate when you are doing that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can help you, Mr. Berikoff, and if you just go to the entries for the 13th and 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: When we went up to Strmica on those days, in fact, it was upped HV control. Whether it was ARSK prior to those day, I'm not sure. Immediately, on the 4th and 5th, I assume that it still would have been under ARSK control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, in fact, if we go back to P744, and go to the entry on page 4 of this document, for 1500, it's noted here that -- do you see that? "ARSK soldiers of unknown strength were seen occupying defensive positions in the general area of Strmica."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's on the 5th, then I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we can go back to this aerial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That was P746.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berikoff, focussing on these blue areas that you have designated, where you saw evidence of artillery fire, as you sit here, sir, the artillery damage that you looked at, given what you've just seen, you have no idea which army, the HV or the ARSK, shot the actual shell that you observed. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROY BERIKOFF
utterances.text: No, I don't, and I don't think there is many people would unless they physically did the firing themselves, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's take that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see there is a collective looking at the clock by the Gotovina Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you don't have to apologise for looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's kind of like, you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would have one concluding question, I would allow you; but if you enter a new area, then I think it would be wiser to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't want to mislead you, Judge. I have a few concluding questions in this area, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn soon. But, Mr. Berikoff, first of all, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether it is the testimony you've given today or the testimony still to be given tomorrow or day after tomorrow. I will explore that with the Defence on how much time will still be needed. Mr. Kehoe, could you give us any indication as far as time is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... finish sometime in the second session tomorrow at the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Other Defence counsel. Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have approximately two hours, no more, and I hope to be significantly less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously, depending on what is covered before me, an hour and a half, at the most, probably less given the ground that will be covered, which I assume will be the same as I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So there is a fair chance, if I also looks at Mr. Russo who might have some questions as well, the Bench may have some questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we will not finish by tomorrow, Mr. Berikoff. I do not know what you expected, but it is it unlikely that we will not finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been given a heads up on that it may go into Thursday, so I am prepared for that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, from the submissions, it might well be that we can conclude your testimony on Wednesday. We adjourn until tomorrow, Tuesday, the 2nd of September, 9.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of September, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
